prompt: A restaurant group studies online reviews of its restaurants. Which limitation of user-generated content does each problem show?

cases.text: Most reviews give one star or five stars, although guests surveyed after their meals mostly rate the visit a three or a four.
cases.explanation: Guests with extreme experiences are more likely to post, so ratings concentrate at the highest and lowest values.

cases.text: Reviews on a photo-sharing app come almost entirely from diners under 30, while most of the group's guests are over 45.
cases.explanation: The users of each platform differ demographically from the population and from the users of other platforms.

cases.text: Forty five-star reviews posted in one week use nearly identical sentences, from accounts created that week.
cases.explanation: Fake reviews and automated accounts, including those that use language models to write text, distort the content.

cases.text: The analyst collected only the reviews the site displays first, which the site ranks by its own measure of helpfulness.
cases.explanation: Platform algorithms determine visibility, so the reviews collected may not represent all those published.

cases.text: A manager reports that 64% of the group's customers like the new menu, because 64% of reviews mentioning it are positive.
cases.explanation: Reviewers chose to post; they are not a probability sample, so the 64% cannot be projected to the customer base with a known precision.

prompt: Each manager holds a large collection of customer text. Which method suits each decision?

cases.text: A brand sponsored a football tournament and wants to know whether posts about it became more favorable in the following month.
cases.explanation: The decision needs the overall favorability of the conversation and its trend after a campaign.

cases.text: A headphone maker wants to know whether reviewers complain more about comfort, sound or battery life.
cases.explanation: The decision concerns specific product attributes, so sentiment is needed toward each attribute mentioned.

cases.text: A gym chain has 6,000 open-ended answers from former members and no list of reasons in mind.
cases.explanation: The relevant themes are not known in advance, so they are identified from the texts themselves.

cases.text: A bank wants each incoming email sent to the fraud, card or mortgage team.
cases.explanation: The categories are known in advance and every message must be assigned to one of them.

cases.text: A hotel chain wants to know which features of its rooms, such as the beds, the Wi-Fi or the showers, generate complaints.
cases.explanation: The question is about particular attributes, so each attribute's sentiment is measured separately.

prompt: An insurer will use a language model to classify claim emails. Put the validation steps in order.

steps.text: Draw a random sample of 500 claim emails.
steps.explanation: Validation starts from a random sample of the collection.

steps.text: Two staff code the sample independently; measure their agreement.
steps.explanation: Human coding is the standard, and its own reliability is checked first.

steps.text: Run the language model on the same 500 emails.
steps.explanation: The automated method codes the same sample the people coded.

steps.text: Report precision and recall for each claim category.
steps.explanation: The automated coding is compared with the human coding, category by category.

steps.text: Check whether accuracy differs for French and English emails.
steps.explanation: Accuracy can differ across products, customer groups or languages.
Consumers' language and the model's behavior change over time.

question_text: A report on a pharmacy chain quotes a public forum post word for word, with the author's username removed: "My pharmacist at the Elm Street store told everyone in line about my insulin prescription." What is the problem?
hint: Think about what a reader could do with the exact words.
correct_answer_citation: Week 12 · Privacy in Text and Social Data

options.option_text: None: the post was public, so the firm may quote it in any report it writes.
options.option_explanation: Publicly accessible content is not free to use for any purpose; platform terms, law and the author's reasonable expectations limit it.

options.option_text: None: once the username is removed, the quotation cannot identify anyone.
options.option_explanation: Removing names does not anonymize a text.

options.option_text: Its exact words can be searched to find the author, and it reveals a health condition.
options.option_explanation: Correct. A verbatim quotation can be located with a search engine, and health is a special category that requires additional protection; the quotation is paraphrased or used with permission.

options.option_text: Keep the quotation, but add the store's postal code and the author's age.
options.option_explanation: Combinations of individually harmless characteristics can also identify an individual.

prompt: These sentences come from a report on a meal-kit company's falling orders. Is each a finding, a conclusion or a recommendation?

cases.text: Customers who skipped three or more weeks fell from 18% to 31% of subscribers after the menu change.
cases.explanation: It states what the data show.

cases.text: The smaller menu is the main reason that subscribers order less often.
cases.explanation: It interprets the findings in relation to the research problem.

cases.text: Restore eight recipes a week in one region, and compare orders there with the other regions before restoring them everywhere.
cases.explanation: It proposes an action on the basis of the conclusions.

cases.text: Of 400 lapsed subscribers surveyed, 46% chose "not enough variety" as their main reason.
cases.explanation: A result from the data, with no interpretation added.

cases.text: Price is not what is driving the decline in orders.
cases.explanation: It interprets findings about the problem; it proposes no action.

prompt: An insights team plans studies of AI shopping agents. Which question of the research agenda does each study address?

cards.text: Does showing the price per kilogram on the product page change which detergent an agent buys?
cards.explanation: It tests how the presentation of information in the storefront affects agents' choices.

cards.text: Which product details does an agent open before buying, when each look takes time?
cards.explanation: It asks which product information agents acquire.

cards.text: Does a retailer's agent recommend its own store brand more often than a shopper's own agent does?
cards.explanation: It asks whether recommendations change with the party the agent serves.

cards.text: Does labeling a listing "Sponsored" change how often agents recommend it?
cards.explanation: It asks whether sponsorship disclosures protect consumers when an agent reads them.

cards.text: When asked for the best running shoes, how often does an assistant include our brand among the options?
cards.explanation: It measures whether the brand is included in the alternatives AI assistants present.

cards.text: In which place, and with which features, does an assistant list our brand?
cards.explanation: It measures the brand's position and the attributes shown with it.
